name: Canberra Times cryptic crossword, Wednesday 22 October 1986

indicators.note: heard means the name is taken by its sound, then written in a different spelling

blocks.note: a girl's name, Sybil
a worker ant

explanation.surface: A woman overheard a labourer making a hissing noise.
explanation.definitionFit: Sibilant describes a hissing sound such as s or sh, so the adjective means hissing.

clue.text: Stop on Sunday, by the river

blocks.note: S is the abbreviation for Sunday
the Tay, Scotland's longest river

explanation.surface: A Sunday halt by the riverbank.
explanation.definitionFit: To stay is to remain or stop somewhere, so it can stand for stop as a verb.

clue.text: Opera opening with singular 7: King George is taking me in

indicators.note: to take something in is to hold it inside, so the next word goes within the one before

blocks.note: Georgius Rex, King George's royal cipher
taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: An opera libretto opening in which a king takes the stage.
explanation.walkthrough: 7 is PETERS; made singular it is PETER, and Britten's opera is Peter Grimes, so the title is PETER followed by this word.
explanation.definitionFit: Peter Grimes is Benjamin Britten's opera, so this word completes a title that begins with the singular footballer name.

clue.text: Having only short sleeps, beast erected bridge

definitions.note: the answer is a verb, has short sleeps

indicators.note: in a down clue, erected means set upright, so the word is read from bottom to top

blocks.note: a cat is a beast
a span is the arch of a bridge

explanation.surface: An animal that dozes in short bursts built a bridge.
explanation.definitionFit: A catnap is a brief doze, so someone who catnaps has only short sleeps.

clue.text: Machine taken from pub - sheik involved

indicators.note: involved means tangled up, so the letters of the words before it are mixed together

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A device removed from a bar with an Arab chief implicated.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Machine' is old slang for a bicycle, which is why a push-bike can be defined this way.
explanation.definitionFit: A pedal bicycle has long been called a machine by cyclists, so the definition is a slang synonym.

clue.text: Strife, though no side sins terribly

indicators.note: terribly means badly done, so the words before it are scrambled into a new order

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Conflict breaks out even though neither team transgressed badly.
explanation.definitionFit: Dissension is disagreement and discord, a noun synonym of strife.

blocks.note: a pet is a favourite
ER, Elizabeth Regina, with the possessive s

explanation.surface: The monarch's top-ranked favourite player.
explanation.walkthrough: 'First' tells you the favourite goes before the Queen's. Martin Peters was an England 1966 World Cup winner.
explanation.definitionFit: Martin Peters was a famous English footballer for West Ham, Tottenham and England.

definitions.note: a place in Australia: the state

blocks.note: first meaning: Manchester's railway terminus of this name
second meaning: the south-eastern Australian state

explanation.surface: It reads like directions to a railway station somewhere in Australia.
explanation.walkthrough: 11 is MANCHESTER, so the first half asks for a Manchester station: Manchester Victoria. The second half is the Australian state of the same name.
explanation.definitionFit: Manchester Victoria is a major railway terminus, and Victoria is also a state of south-east Australia, capital Melbourne.

definitions.note: the club name minus its city

blocks.note: first meaning: Manchester's football club with this second name
second meaning: brought together as one

explanation.surface: A footballer signs for a club in the city of 11.
explanation.walkthrough: 11 is MANCHESTER; the football club is Manchester United FC, and 'joined' doubles as the plain-English meaning of the same word.
explanation.definitionFit: United is a past participle meaning combined or brought together, and it is the second word of Manchester's most famous club.

definitions.note: the club name minus its city
used as an adjective, as in city life

blocks.note: first meaning: Manchester's other football club, the Sky Blues
second meaning: of a large town, used attributively

explanation.surface: An urban football club from the city of 11.
explanation.walkthrough: 11 is MANCHESTER, whose second football club is Manchester City FC; the word is also used attributively for anything urban, as in city streets.
explanation.definitionFit: As a modifier the noun describes things belonging to a large town, which is the meaning of urban.

definitions.note: A phrase standing for a noun: fair because the city is defined as something located in Lancashire, its historic county.

blocks.note: a fellow is a man
Charlie Chester, a British radio and television comedian

explanation.surface: A comic's partner who works in Lancashire.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fellow-comedian' looks like a colleague in comedy; split at the hyphen it is two pieces. Charlie Chester was a well-known British comedian of the 1940s to 1980s.
explanation.definitionFit: Manchester lay in the historic county of Lancashire, so the city is a place found in that county.

indicators.note: the word before turns into something new, so its letters are rearranged into another word

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Going over the main points again leads to fun and games.
explanation.walkthrough: The scan reads 'Redcaps', but no letter of D appears in the answer; the wordplay needs 'Recaps', whose six letters rearrange exactly.
explanation.definitionFit: Capers are playful leaps or pranks, a synonym for frolics as a plural noun.

clue.text: Everton, lacking weight, fractured legs without publicity in America

definitions.note: A phrase standing for a noun: fair because the wetland is defined as something found in America, by location.

indicators.note: lacking means going without something, so one word is removed from the team name
something fractured is broken apart, so the letters are reassembled differently
without here means outside, so one piece wraps round another

blocks.note: the Liverpool football club, taken as written
a ton is a weight
taken as written
an ad, advertisement, is publicity

explanation.surface: An Everton side, out of shape, plays its matches in the USA without any fanfare.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Without publicity' reads as one phrase, but 'without' means outside here, wrapping the scrambled legs around the advert. The weight is removed from the end of the club name.
explanation.definitionFit: The Everglades are the vast subtropical wetlands of southern Florida, a place in the United States.

clue.text: Soft border on cape denotes stiff formality

blocks.note: p, piano, is the musical direction for soft
a rim is an edge or border
a ness is a headland or promontory

explanation.surface: A soft edging on a cloak suggests buttoned-up propriety.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cape' reads as a garment, but here it is a headland: NESS appears in British place names such as Orford Ness.
explanation.definitionFit: Primness is a prudish, starchy correctness of manner, i.e. a stiff formality.

indicators.note: something strange is out of its normal order, so the letters before it are rearranged

blocks.note: the apostrophe is ignored

explanation.surface: The crossword compiler has peculiar habits.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ways' looks like habits or methods, but it means roads, as in thoroughfares.
explanation.definitionFit: Way is a standard word for a road or route, so streets are ways in the thoroughfare sense.

blocks.note: surface reading: the feet of players in the Bolton football team
setter's reading: the club's nickname is also a word for pigs' feet

explanation.walkthrough: Bolton Wanderers, a Lancashire football club, are nicknamed after a word that also means pigs' feet, sold as food; the question mark flags the pun.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means pigs' feet as cooked meat and is also the nickname of Bolton Wanderers football club.

indicators.note: one word is placed inside the other, so the second sits within the first

blocks.note: people, as in men and women
to ride is to travel on a horse or vehicle

explanation.surface: Voters commuting across a seat in central England.
explanation.walkthrough: Meriden is a parliamentary constituency in the West Midlands, between Birmingham and Coventry, traditionally called the centre of England.
explanation.definitionFit: Meriden is an English parliamentary seat lying in the Midlands region.

blocks.note: first meaning: charming, winning
second meaning: gripping, as gears mesh and hold

explanation.walkthrough: Two separate senses of one present participle: charming, and interlocking or gripping, as gears do when they mesh.
explanation.definitionFit: The word describes a charming personality and also the action of gripping or occupying, as in engaging the enemy.

blocks.note: an ass is a fool
ails means is unwell

explanation.surface: An idiot gets ill from bad weather.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Storms' looks like a noun for weather; here it is the verb, as when troops storm a castle.
explanation.definitionFit: To storm a position is to attack it violently, and assails means attacks, both present-tense verbs.

indicators.note: something faltering is unsteady and stumbling, so the letters of the word before it lose their order

blocks.note: to drag is to trail along the ground
the four letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Troops lag behind and soon begin to waver.
explanation.definitionFit: Dragoons were mounted infantry, and the word survives in regimental names, so they are soldiers.

indicators.note: arranged means put in order, so the letters of the word before it are set out afresh
outside means one piece goes around the other one

blocks.note: taken as written
U is the abbreviation for university

explanation.surface: A formal court hearing is set up beyond the campus.
explanation.definitionFit: Ritual as an adjective describes things done as part of a rite or ceremony, matching ceremonial.

blocks.note: taken as written
an age is a long span of years

explanation.surface: A man in charge is getting older.
explanation.definitionFit: To manage something is to run or direct it, so the verb is a synonym of control.

clue.text: Teacher has more versions of New Testament

indicators.note: different versions present the same material another way, so these letters are recombined

blocks.note: taken as written
NT is the standard abbreviation for New Testament

explanation.surface: A schoolmaster owns several translations of the gospels.
explanation.definitionFit: A mentor is a trusted adviser and guide, so the word serves as a synonym for a teacher.

clue.text: Old form of transport for poor team's followers.

indicators.note: a poor version of something is badly put together, so its letters come out in a different order

blocks.note: the apostrophe is ignored
a train is a retinue of followers

explanation.surface: Fans of a struggling side travel to away games by vintage means.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Followers' looks like football supporters, but a train is also the retinue that follows a king or bride.
explanation.definitionFit: Trains hauled by steam locomotives were the standard rail transport before diesel and electric power replaced them.

indicators.note: one piece takes the centre position, so it sits inside the other

blocks.note: re means about or concerning
Ag is the chemical symbol for silver

explanation.surface: Fury at a silver core, perhaps a medal dispute.
explanation.definitionFit: Rage is violent anger, a straightforward synonym as a noun.

blocks.note: first meaning: a small loaf
second meaning: the partner of rock in the music style

explanation.walkthrough: 'Bread with rock' suggests a hard loaf; read instead as the pairing 'rock and ___', the music style of the 1950s.
explanation.definitionFit: A roll is a small individual loaf, and the word completes the phrase rock and roll, the popular music genre.

clue.text: Anxiety brings back engineer with a rush

indicators.note: brought back means turned round, so the abbreviation that follows is read right to left

blocks.note: care is worry or anxiety
RE, the Royal Engineers, a corps of the British Army

explanation.surface: Nerves return when an engineer arrives in a hurry.
explanation.definitionFit: As a verb, to career is to rush headlong at speed, often out of control.

clue.text: See work on equator, where 23 ran

blocks.note: lo, as in lo and behold, means see
op is short for opus, a work
the equator is called the Line

explanation.surface: Watch the work being done along the equator, a route of the 23.
explanation.walkthrough: 'See' wants to be a bishop's see, but it is the old exclamation. 23 is the steam train, which ran on such a branch.
explanation.definitionFit: A loop line is a railway branch leaving the main line and rejoining it, a place where trains ran.
